title: India Banned Telegram for 150 Million Users to Protect One Exam. A Court Just Said That Was Fine.
excerpt: The Delhi High Court upheld the government's unprecedented week-long shutdown of Telegram ahead of the NEET re-exam — setting a precedent that could reshape how India governs tech platforms.
body:
India did something in June that no other major democracy has done in years: it banned an entire messaging platform — used by 150 million people — for a week, because it couldn't trust its own exam system.

Telegram went dark across India on June 16, pulled from the Google Play Store and Apple's App Store under orders from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. The trigger was the NEET-UG medical entrance exam, whose original May 3 sitting had been cancelled after a chemistry lecturer allegedly sold leaked questions through WhatsApp groups for thousands of dollars apiece. With a re-exam scheduled for June 21, the government decided that Telegram's architecture — large public channels, bots, and the ability to edit old posts without changing timestamps — made it too dangerous to leave online.

On June 19, the Delhi High Court agreed.

## What the Court Said

Justice Tejas Karia dismissed Telegram's petition challenging the ban in a 39-page verdict that will be studied by every tech company operating in India. The court found that the government was fully empowered under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act to block the entire platform — not just offending channels — and that the temporary, bounded nature of the restriction satisfied the constitutional test of proportionality.

"Temporarily blocking public access to Telegram cannot be held to be disproportional," Justice Karia wrote.

Telegram had argued that a blanket ban on a platform with 150 million users was wildly disproportionate when the government's real concern was a few hundred channels. The company said it had already removed over 900 links containing unlawful NEET-related content and deployed AI tools to detect more. It wanted the court to order targeted takedowns instead.

The government, represented by Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, pushed back hard. Telegram's features, he argued, made targeted enforcement nearly impossible. Channel administrators could edit previously posted messages while retaining the original timestamp — and could swap attached PDFs after publication. Scammers had exploited exactly this feature after the May 3 exam, editing old posts to insert the actual question paper and then circulating screenshots as "proof" of a pre-exam leak, fooling future test-takers into paying for their services.

## The 35-Page Report Nobody Was Supposed to See

But the exam was only part of the story. During the court proceedings, the Home Ministry's Cybercrime Coordination Centre submitted a 35-page report — not publicly released, but reviewed by Reuters — that went far beyond NEET.

The report found that Telegram was being used extensively to share child sexual abuse material and perpetrate financial scams across India. The government flagged the platform's privacy features, which allow users to interact without revealing a phone number, as a key obstacle to law enforcement. One city's cybercrime investigation alone uncovered nearly $160,000 in financial transactions linked to exam fraud conducted through Telegram channels.

The message was clear: this ban may have been triggered by an exam, but the government's concerns with Telegram run much deeper.

## Pavel Durov Fires Back

Telegram's CEO Pavel Durov was characteristically blunt. "India's IT ministry banned Telegram for one week because some users shared leaked exam questions," he posted on X. "This punishes 150M+ ordinary Telegram users in India — not the insiders who leaked the exam materials. And the ban hasn't stopped anything. The leaks just moved to other apps."

He has a point. As transparency activist Vivek Pandey told the Wall Street Journal: "You banned Telegram. What if they send it via email or WhatsApp or Snapchat?"

The ban was lifted on June 22, the day after the re-exam. But one restriction remains in place: Telegram's message-editing feature is disabled in India until June 30 — a surgical measure that targets the specific exploit the government identified.

## A Precedent That Matters Beyond NEET

India's Telegram ban sits at the intersection of two forces that define the country's relationship with technology: a genuine crisis in exam integrity, and an increasingly assertive regulatory state.

The NEET scandal is staggering in scope. Over 2.27 million students sat for the original May 3 exam. A chemistry lecturer with insider access allegedly ran "special coaching classes" in April where he dictated questions that later appeared on the test. Students paid thousands of dollars to attend. The Central Bureau of Investigation has made arrests, and Rajasthan police have traced the leaked "guess paper" to a medical student from Sikar studying in Kerala, from where it cascaded through hostel owners, coaching centres, and WhatsApp groups across multiple states.

The government's response has been unusually aggressive. Telegram was banned. The re-exam on June 21 deployed military-grade security: exam paper transporters were given armed escorts, question papers were digitally encrypted until minutes before the test began, and personnel involved in question-setting were isolated at secure facilities with limited device access.

But it also set a troubling precedent. The Internet Freedom Foundation called the ban unconstitutional and an overreach. "If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour," the organisation argued, "and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available."

India is not the only country to shut off digital access during exams — Syria and Sudan have done so too. But India is the world's largest digital market. Its willingness to ban a platform used by 150 million people, and to have that ban survive judicial review, sends a signal to every tech company from Silicon Valley to Shenzhen.

## What Comes Next

The Telegram ban is over, but its aftershocks are just beginning. Congress has announced a 40-day nationwide campaign titled "Chhatron Ki Goonj" (Voice of Students), starting June 30, demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation and a complete overhaul of the examination system. Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk has announced an indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar over NEET accountability and Ladakh's environmental protection. The Cockroach Janta Party, a satirical online movement turned real protest platform, has been camped at Jantar Mantar since June 20, its founder — a 30-year-old Boston University graduate — refusing to leave until the education minister resigns.

The NTA has released provisional answer keys for the June 21 re-exam and is processing OMR scans. Results are expected soon. But for 23 lakh students who've spent years preparing for this one test, the damage runs deeper than any app ban can fix. Three students have died by suicide since the original paper leak was confirmed.

India banned Telegram to protect an exam. Whether it can fix the system that made the ban necessary is the question that matters.

Sources: Reuters, Wall Street Journal, Delhi High Court verdict (June 19, 2026), Hindu Business Line, Bar and Bench, Medianama, CNN
